title: Fast Walking Helps Health, Even Below 10,000 Steps
paragraphs: Many people try to walk 10,000 steps a day to stay healthy. However, a new study suggests that how fast you walk may be just as important as how many steps you take, and that walking briskly can bring health benefits even if you do not reach 10,000 steps.

The study was published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in September 2026. Researchers analyzed data on 64,743 adults in the UK, who had an average age of 61.5. The participants wore activity trackers on their wrists for seven days, which recorded both how many steps they took and how fast they walked. The researchers then followed them for about eight years. During that period, 1,697 of the participants died.

The researchers found that the lowest risk of death was among people who took between 7,500 and 10,000 steps a day at a brisk pace of about 100 steps per minute. However, they also found that walking speed made a big difference for people who were less active. Among those taking fewer than 5,000 steps a day, people who walked faster during their most active half-hour had a 25% to 33% lower risk of dying than people who took the same number of steps slowly. In fact, their risk was similar to that of people who took between 5,000 and 7,500 steps at a slower pace.
Interestingly, the researchers pointed out that the popular 10,000-step goal did not come from science. Instead, it came from a marketing campaign for a Japanese pedometer in the 1960s.

According to Koemel, a senior research fellow at Monash University in Australia and one of the researchers, there is no single step target that is right for everyone. Koemel suggested that for people who are short on time, walking faster may be a good first goal.
However, the study was observational, so it cannot prove that walking faster directly helps people live longer.
